body: Building a supply of high-quality child care that meets the needs and preferences of parents participating in CCDF is necessary to meet CCDF’s core purposes. Lead Agencies must support parent choice by providing some portion of direct services via grants or contracts, including at a minimum for children in underserved geographic areas, infants and toddlers, and children with disabilities. 4.5.1 Child care services available through grants or contracts Does the Lead Agency provide direct child care services through grants or contracts for child care slots? [ ] Yes, statewide. Describe how the Lead Agency ensures that parents who enroll with a provider who has a grant or contract have choices when selecting a provider: [x] Yes, in some jurisdictions, but not statewide. Describe how many jurisdictions use grants or contracts for child care slots and how the Lead Agency ensures that parents who enroll with a provider who has a grant or contract have choices when selecting a provider: Under CCCAP, each county has the option of developing slot contracts with licensed child care centers and family child care homes. Two counties are currently approved to offer slot contracts. [ ] No. If no, describe any Lead Agency plans to provide direct child care services through grants and contracts for child care slots: If no, skip to question 4.5.2. i. If yes, identify the populations of children served through grants or contracts for child care slots (check all that apply). For each population selected, identify the number of slots allocated through grants or contracts for direct service of children receiving CCDF. [ ] Children with disabilities. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [x] Infants and toddlers. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: As of 5/13/2024, 3 slots are allocated for children ages 0-36 months who are also engaged in a child welfare program. [ ] Children in underserved geographic areas. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children needing non-traditional hour care. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] School-age children. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children experiencing homelessness. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children in urban areas. Percent of CCDF children served in an average month: [ ] Children in rural areas. Percent of CCDF children served in an average month: [x] Other populations. If checked, describe: As of 5/13/2024, 4 slots are allocated for children ages 36 months to school age that are also engaged in a child welfare program. ii. If yes, how are rates for slots funded by grants and contracts determined by the Lead Agency? Rates are funded through county allocations for slot contracts. 4.5.2 Care in the child’s home (in-home care) The Lead Agency must allow for in-home care (i.e., care provided in the child’s own home) but may limit its use. Will the Lead Agency limit the use of in-home care in any way? [x] Yes. [ ] No. If yes, what limits will the Lead Agency set on the use of in-home care? Check all that apply. i. [ ] Restricted based on the minimum number of children in the care of the in- home provider to meet the Fair Labor Standards Act (minimum wage) requirements. Describe: ii. [ ] Restricted based on the in-home provider meeting a minimum age requirement. Describe: iii. [ ] Restricted based on the hours of care (i.e., certain number of hours, non- traditional work hours). Describe: iv. [x] Restricted to care by relatives. (A relative provider must be at least 18 years of age based on the definition of eligible child care provider.) Describe: Relative CCCAP Qualified Exempt Providers may be approved to provide care in the child’s home. v. [ ] Restricted to care for children with special needs or a medical condition. Describe: vi. [ ] Restricted to in-home providers that meet additional health and safety requirements beyond those required by CCDF. Describe: vii. [ ] Other. Describe: 4.5.3 Shortages in the supply of child care Lead Agencies must identify shortages in the supply of child care providers that meet parents’ needs and preferences. What child care shortages has the Lead Agency identified in the State or Territory, and what is the plan to address the child care shortages? a. In infant and toddler programs: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Child care licensing data; Colorado population data from the US Census and State Demographer’s Office projections; surveys and reports conducted by other organizations in Colorado. It is important to note that it is currently impossible to measure demand directly in Colorado because there is no reliable, real-time data on demand. CDEC’s licensed capacity data is the most reliable, consistent data that speaks to the breadth of the child care landscape in Colorado. As part of a federally-funded Preschool Development Grant (PDG) effort in 2019, a Needs Assessment was conducted in Colorado that illustrated a shortage of child care options in Colorado, particularly among infants and toddlers. This report indicated that nearly 39,000 more children under 5 would be cared for in licensed care in Colorado if appropriate, affordable licensed child care options were available. It also concluded that only 14% and 16% of infants and toddlers, respectively, in Colorado can be cared for in existing licensed child care. The need for additional child care options in the infant/toddler space was emphasized by the most recent Needs Assessment conducted in 2023, which involved reviewing various surveys and reports in Colorado’s early childhood space as well as new data collection from partner groups. ii. Method of tracking progress: CDEC produces internal annual capacity maps to illustrate the maximum percentage of a county’s estimated child population that could be served by licensed child care providers if optimal conditions are met, with a breakdown for high-quality care. CDEC also reports on the proportion of high-quality providers in the publicly-available licensed child care facilities report on the Colorado Information Marketplace. To address the gaps in infant and toddler care, the Department used $7 million in stimulus funding to shift to enrollment based payment for infants and toddlers in CCCAP, which resulted in cumulative additional 566 children enrolled in this age group. Also, increasing infant and toddler care is one of CDEC's wildly important goals, and progress on increasing infant and toddler capacity is tracked monthly. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes We are incentivizing providers to open and operate early childhood programs through our Emerging and Expanding grant program. Family child care providers may apply to expand their home based programs or to open new sites. Grants are available up to $50,000 and are funded through State and Local Fiscal Recovery funding (SLFRF). Additionally, Colorado funds a position within Early Childhood Councils to support Family Childcare Home providers. The FCCH Navigator role works with providers to provide support and TA in navigating the licensing process, quality process, and supports them with locating grant funding as needed to stand up or expand their program. iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? There are two active grant programs within Colorado funded through SLFRF to address child care supply in Colorado. The first is the Emerging and Expanding grant program that supports programs with grants up to $200,000 to build new or expand an existing program. The second grant opportunity is targeted to employers to build or contract for onsite or near site child care for their employees and the community. The Employer-Based Child Care grant program offers grant opportunities up to $800,000 and requires a percentage match. b. In different regions of the State or Territory: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Child care licensing data; Colorado population data from the US Census and State Demographer’s Office projections all at the county level; Surveys and reports conducted by other organizations in Colorado. ii. Method of tracking progress: We produce internal annual capacity maps to illustrate the maximum percentage of a county’s estimated child population that could be served by licensed child care providers if optimal conditions are met, with a breakdown for high-quality care. We also report on the proportion of high- quality providers in our publicly available licensed child care facilities report on the Colorado Information Marketplace. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes? CDEC seeks to ensure all families have equitable access to high-quality early care and learning so that all children start school ready to succeed. The activities Colorado is, or has, invested in that are designed to increase the number of licensed programs, improve the quality of licensed programs, ensure equitable access for underserved families, and sustain services by closing the revenue- expenditure gap can be found in the strategies to improve access and quality section of the Investing in Early Childhood website. https://sites.google.com/state.co.us/cdec-stimulus-grant-activity/home iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? CDEC seeks to ensure all families have equitable access to high-quality early care and learning so that all children start school ready to succeed. The activities Colorado is, or has, invested in that are designed to increase the number of licensed programs, improve the quality of licensed programs, ensure equitable access for underserved families, and sustain services by closing the revenue- expenditure gap can be found in the strategies to improve access and quality section of the Investing in Early Childhood website. https://sites.google.com/state.co.us/cdec-stimulus-grant-activity/home c. In care for special populations: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Surveys and focus groups conducted by contracted vendors and the CDEC Needs Assessment. ii. Method of tracking progress: We produce internal annual capacity maps to illustrate the maximum percentage of a county’s estimated child population that could be served by licensed child care providers. We also report monthly on child care capacity across the state and the number of bilingual Spanish child care providers. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes? Our most recent Needs Assessment conducted in 2023 synthesized several reports, surveys, and other resources across Colorado and identified additional areas where care shortages may exist. This review concluded that children with special health needs or disabilities in Colorado need more child care options, but the state does not yet collect data to provide actionable insight into where these needs are most pronounced. This assessment also highlighted a need for child care options that accommodate languages other than English and Spanish. These findings will be used to engage with the broader early childhood community across the state to identify areas to focus collective impact in Colorado. iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? Our most recent Needs Assessment conducted in 2023 synthesized several reports, surveys, and other resources across Colorado and identified additional areas where care shortages may exist. This review concluded that children with special health needs or disabilities in Colorado need more child care options, but the state does not yet collect data to provide actionable insight into where these needs are most pronounced. This assessment also highlighted a need for child care options that accommodate languages other than English and Spanish. These findings will be used to engage with the broader Early Childhood community of Colorado to identify areas to focus collective impact in Colorado. 4.5.4 Strategies to increase the supply of and improve quality of child care Lead Agencies must develop and implement strategies to increase the supply of and improve the quality of child care services. These strategies must address child care in underserved geographic areas; infants and toddlers; children with disabilities, as defined by the Lead Agency; and children who receive care during non-traditional hours. How does the Lead Agency identify any gaps in the supply and quality of child care services and what strategies are used to address those gaps for: a. Underserved geographic areas. Describe: CDEC contracts with Early Childhood Councils to recruit and retain providers as well as support quality improvement - particularly in underserved areas. Additionally, under the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program (CCCAP), each county has the option of developing contracts for slots with licensed child care centers and family child care homes. Contracts for slots serve the purposes of increasing supply, quality and serving vulnerable and underserved families. Tiered reimbursement rates are available to programs participating in CCCAP and Colorado Shines ratings. Higher ratings are awarded with higher CCCAP reimbursement rates. CDEC has two grant funded opportunities to assist in communities with addressing capacity gaps, funded with state and local fiscal recovery funding (SLFRF). The Emerging and Expanding grant program supports providers to expand their programs to create capacity in underserved areas, considered child care deserts. It also supports new programs to open within these areas. Funding from this grant can be used for start-up costs that include capital expenditures. The second grant program is the Employer-Based Child Care program. This grant opportunity is for employers who want to expand options for their employees to have onsite or near site child care options and subsidizes this cost for their employees. Technical Assistance is offered to child care providers by CDEC’s licensing team and Early Childhood Councils, particularly those in underserved areas, rural areas and those with unique challenges. b. Infants and toddlers. Describe: CDEC contracts with Early Childhood Councils to recruit and retain providers as well as support quality improvement statewide, with infant and toddler care as an identified priority area. Additionally, under the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program (CCCAP), each county has the option of developing contracts for slots with licensed child care centers and family child care homes. Contracts for slots serve the purposes of increasing supply, quality and serving vulnerable and underserved families. Tiered reimbursements rates are available to programs participating in CCCAP and Colorado Shines ratings. Higher ratings are awarded with higher CCCAP reimbursements rates, including a higher base rate for infant and toddler care. The Emerging and Expanding grant program was established to address capacity shortages across the state, especially in those areas of the state that have been identified as child care deserts. The entire state of Colorado is considered a desert for infant and toddler capacity shortages. This grant prioritizes applications that are expanding infant and toddler capacity. c. Children with disabilities. Describe: CDEC contracts with Early Childhood Councils to recruit and retain providers as well as support quality improvement statewide, which must include serving families with children with disabilities. Additionally, under the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program (CCCAP), each county has the option of developing contracts for slots with licensed child care centers and family child care homes. Contracts for slots serve the purpose of increasing supply and quality and serving vulnerable and underserved families. CDEC contracts with the state’s child care resource and referral agencies to provide technical assistance for providers, including those serving children with special needs. In addition, through the Colorado Early Learning: Universal Design & Inclusion Project, https://www.ucdenver.edu/centers/center-for-inclusive-design-and- engineering/community-engagement/pdg CDEC contracts with the Center for Inclusive Design and Engineering at the University of Colorado to provide child care programs with intensive support on adapting materials and environments to ensure early learning is accessible for children with delays and disabilities. These include licensed centers and family child care homes that accept CCCAP and such providers are prioritized for acceptance into the cohort. Over six months, participating providers receive: a training on Inclusion and Universal Design; a training series addressing how to adapt materials and environments to address delays or disabilities in the various domains (i.e. communication, gross motor, etc.); reflection sessions and ongoing coaching to ensure lessons learned are incorporated into the program; a kit with materials and instructions to create low-tech adaptations; and access to a lending library of low-tech assistive technology, materials, and resources. d. Children who receive care during non-traditional hours. Describe: Under the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program (CCCAP), each county has the option of developing contracts for slots with licensed child care centers and family child care homes and can select a target population that includes non-traditional care. Contracts for slots serve the purpose of increasing supply and quality and serving vulnerable and underserved families. Counties have the option to set rates for non-traditional care above the State-Established daily rate to address shortages in the supply and availability of this care. e. Other. Specify what population is being focused on to increase supply or improve quality. Describe: 4.5.5 Prioritization of investments in areas of concentrated poverty and unemployment Lead Agencies must prioritize investments for increasing access to high-quality child care and development services for children of families in areas that have significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment and do not currently have sufficient numbers of such programs. Describe how the Lead Agency prioritizes increasing access to high-quality child care and development services for children of families in areas that have significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment and that do not have access to high-quality programs. CDEC uses data that considers high concentrations of poverty and unemployment in areas that lack high-quality child care as a factor to inform the award of quality improvement funds. Information reported from providers is used to formulate a high-needs score. The high-needs score is determined through the calculation of points for program level enrollment data and community-level census data for high-needs categories. Enrollment data is self-reported within the provider’s profile, this information is updated twice annually. Programs report enrollment counts for children receiving tuition support from one or more of the following funding sources: Colorado Child Care Assistance Program, Head Start/Early Head Start, and Colorado’s Universal Pre-Kindergarten program. In addition, programs report enrollment counts for children receiving services and support through an individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) or Individualized Education Program (IEP). Programs also receive points based on community level scores for the following high needs categories: Census data is uploaded to the Colorado Shines Quality Rating and Improvement System database to inform the community level score for a program. Factors include percentage of child care subsidy enrollments, years of operation, quality rating level (where higher points are assigned to lower quality rating levels), whether a program uses a formal curriculum and /or child assessment approach, staff professional development, and the capacity of the program to expand slots for children receiving child care subsidy. Early Childhood Councils, as the local implementation partner for quality improvement programming, use the high needs score to prioritize applications for quality improvement funds. 5 Health and Safety of Child Care Settings Child care health and safety standards and enforcement practices are essential to protect the health and safety of children while out of their parents’ care. CCDF provides a minimum threshold for child care health and safety policies and practices but leaves authority to Lead Agencies to design standards that appropriately protect children’s safety and promote nurturing environments that support their healthy growth and development. Lead Agencies should set standards for ratios, group size limits, and provider qualifications that help ensure that the child care environment is conducive to safety and learning and enable caregivers to promote all domains of children’s development. CCDF health and safety standards help set clear expectations for CCDF providers, form the foundation for health and safety training for child care workers, and establish the baseline for monitoring to ensure compliance with health and safety requirements. These health and safety requirements apply to all providers serving children receiving CCDF services – whether the providers are licensed or license-exempt, must be appropriate to the provider setting and age of the children served, must include specific topics and training on those topics, and are subject to monitoring and enforcement procedures by the Lead Agency. CCDF-required annual monitoring and enforcement actions help ensure that CCDF providers are adopting and implementing health and safety requirements. Through child care licensing, Lead Agencies set minimum requirements, including health and safety requirements, that child care providers must meet to legally operate in that State or Territory. In some cases, CCDF health and safety requirements may be integrated within the licensing system for licensed providers and may be separate for CCDF providers who are license- exempt. This section addresses CCDF health and safety requirements, Lead Agency licensing requirements and exemptions, and comprehensive background checks. When responding to questions in this section, OCC recognizes that each Lead Agency identifies and defines its own categories of care. OCC does not expect Lead Agencies to change their definitions to fit the CCDF-defined categories of care. For these questions, provide responses that best match the CCDF categories of care.

The term includes, but is not limited to, facilities commonly known as child care centers, school-age child care centers, before- and after-school programs, kindergartens, preschools, day camps, and summer camps. Exemptions for relative providers will be addressed in subsection 5.8. 5.2.1 Age classifications Describe how the Lead Agency defines the following age classifications (e.g., Infant: 0 – 18 months). a. Infant. Describe: The age definition of an infant is six weeks to 18 months old. Overlap between ages infant/toddler/preschool are to allow time for transition appropriate to the child's development. b. Toddler. Describe: The age definition of a toddler is 12 months to 36 months old. Overlap between ages infant/toddler/preschool are to allow time for transition appropriate to the child's development. c. Preschool. Describe: The age definition of a preschooler is two and a half through six years of age. Overlap between ages infant/toddler/preschool are to allow time for transition appropriate to the child's development. d. School-Age. Describe: The age range for school-age children is five (5) and eighteen (18) years of age. Licensed center-based care i. Qualifications for staff in Infant programs, toddler programs, preschool, and school-age programs are covered below: In Colorado, an early childhood teacher, assigned responsibility for a single group of children and working under the supervision of a director, must be at least eighteen years of age and meet at least one of the following qualifications: a. Twenty-one months (3,185 hours) of verified experience in the care and supervision of four or more children less than eight years of age who are not related to the individual. Satisfactory experience includes being a licensee of a Colorado family child care home, a teacher’s aide or teacher in a child care center, preschool, or elementary school. In addition, the individual must either: 1) Possess a current early childhood professional credential level I or higher in version 3.0 as determined by the Department; or 2) Complete two three-semester credit hour courses from an accredited college or university in early childhood education with one course as either: a) Introduction to early childhood professions or has been issued the Child Development Associate (CDA) credential; or b) Early childhood guidance strategies for children or has been issued a Colorado Pyramid Model training certificate of completion. Infant Program Staff The infant program must have an infant program supervisor who meets at least one of the following qualifications: 1) A Registered Nurse, with an active license from the Colorado State Board of Nursing, with a minimum of three months (455 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of infants who are not related to the individual; 2) A Licensed Practical Nurse, with an active license from the Colorado State Board of Nursing, a minimum of nine months (1,365 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of infants who are not related to the individual; 3) An adult who holds a certificate in infant and toddler care from an accredited college or university with completion of a minimum of thirty (30) semester credit hours in the development and care of infants and toddlers in a group setting; 4) An adult who is currently certified as a child development associate (CDA) in: center-based, preschool; center-based, infant-toddler; or family child care; and has completed the infant/toddler theory and practice or has been issued the expanding quality in infant and toddler care training certificate of completion; 5) An adult who holds a current early childhood professional credential level II or higher in version 3.0, as determined by the Department, has a minimum of nine months (1,365 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of infants and/or toddlers, and: a) Has completed one three semester credit hour course in infant/toddler development; or b) Has completed the Department-approved expanding quality in infant and toddler care training course. 6) An adult who: a) Is at least nineteen years of age; b) Is qualified as an early childhood teacher; c) Has a minimum of nine months (1,365 hours) of verifiable experience in the group care of infants or toddlers; and d) Has completed at least two three-semester credit hour courses from an accredited college or university on the development and care of infants and toddlers in a group setting, one of which must be: i) Infant/Toddler Development; or ii) CDEC-approved expanding quality in infant and toddler care training course. 7) An adult who: a) Is at least nineteen years of age; b) Is qualified as an early childhood teacher; c) Has a minimum of one year and nine months (3,185 hours) of verifiable experience in the group care and supervision of infants or toddlers; and d) Will complete, within the first six (6) months of employment, two three- semester credit hour courses from an accredited college or university, one of which must be: i) Infant/Toddler development; or ii) CDEC-approved expanding quality in infant and toddler care training course. An infant program early childhood teacher must meet the following requirements: 1) Meet the qualifications for an early childhood teacher, or be qualified as an infant program supervisor; and 2) Has a minimum of three months (455 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of children under three years of age. Prior to being assigned a group of children, the infant program early childhood teacher must complete eight hours of orientation in the infant program under the supervision of the infant program supervisor. The orientation may include, but not be limited to, the following topics: a) Toys and equipment, appropriate activities for infants and toddlers, appropriate sleep positions for infants and toddlers, and the safe and appropriate diaper change technique. Toddler Program Staff The toddler early childhood teacher, a staff member assigned responsibility for a single group and working under the supervision of the director, must meet at least one of the following qualifications: A Registered Nurse, licensed to practice in Colorado, with a minimum of three months (455 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of children less than three years of age who are not related to the individual; A Licensed Practical Nurse, licensed to practice in Colorado, with at least nine months (1,365 hours) of verifiable experience in the care and supervision of children less than three years of age who are not related to the individual; An adult who holds a certificate in infant and toddler care from an accredited college or university with completion of at least thirty semester credit hours or equivalent in such courses as child growth and development, nutrition, and care practices with children birth to three years of age; An adult who is certified as a child development associate (CDA) in: center-based, preschool; center-based, infant-toddler; or family child care; or is certified as a child care professional (CCP); or holds another Department-approved certificate; An adult who meets the education and experience requirements for an early childhood teacher of a large center (rule section 2.216(A)); or A current early childhood professional credential level II or higher in version 3.0 as determined by the Department. School-age Child Care Center Staff Program Leaders 1) Each program leader must be at least eighteen (18) years of age, demonstrate ability to work with children, and must meet the following qualifications: a. Must have at least three (3) months (455 hours) of verified experience in the care and supervision of four (4) or more children over the ages of four (4) who are not related to the individual. b. A current early childhood professional credential level I (1) or higher in version 3.0 as determined by the Department. ii. Describe the director qualification for licensed CCDF center-based care, including any variations based on the ages of children in care or the number of staff employed: In Colorado, there is no variation of qualifications for directors based on the ages of children in care or the number of staff employed. DIRECTOR QUALIFICATIONS - LARGE CHILD CARE CENTER (16 or more children) Large center directors must have a current director qualifications letter issued by CDEC or a current early childhood professional credential level III or higher in version 3.0 as determined by CDEC prior to working as the director of a large center. The educational requirements for the director of a large center must be met by satisfactory completion of one of the following. A Bachelor’s, Master’s, or Doctorate degree from an accredited college or university in one of the following: Child Development Child Psychology Early Childhood Education Early Childhood Special Education Educational Leadership and Administration Elementary Education Family and Human Development Family Studies Special Education 2) Completion of all of the following three semester credit hour courses from an accredited college or university in each of the following subject or content areas: a. Introduction to Early Childhood Professions b. Introduction to Early Childhood Techniques c. Guidance Strategies for Young Children or has been issued the Colorado Pyramid Model Training certificate of completion d. Health, Nutrition, and Safety e. Administration of Early Childhood Care and Education Programs f. Administration: Human Relations for Early Childhood Professions or Introduction to Business g. Curriculum Development: Methods and Techniques h. Child Growth and Development i. The Exceptional Child j. Infant/Toddler Theory and Practice or have been issued the Expanding Quality Infant/Toddler Training certificate of completion 3) Completion of a course of training approved by the Department that includes course content listed at rule section 2.214(B)(1), and experience listed at rule section 2.214(C). The experience requirements for the director of a large center must include direct work with young children within an early care and education setting and is based on the completion of the following amount of verified work experience in the care and supervision of four or more children less than eight years of age who are not related to the individual: 1) Persons with a Bachelor’s, Master’s, or Doctorate degree with a major emphasis as listed in rule section 2.214(B)(1), or individuals with an early childhood professional credential level III version 3.0 as determined by the Department; no additional experience is required. 2) Persons with an Associate’s degree in early childhood education or child development must have three (3) months (455 hours) of verified experience. 3) Persons with a Bachelor's degree and have completed the thirty semester credit hours specified in rule section 2.214(B)(2), must have three months (455 hours) of verified experience. 4) Persons who have no degree but have completed the thirty (30) semester credit hours specified in rule section 2.214(B)(2), must have six months (910 hours) of verified experience. 5) Additional requirements for verified experience include: a. Verified experience acquired in a school-age child care center may count for up to half of the required experience for director qualifications. The other half of the required experience must be working directly with children in a child development program; and, b. For family child care home experience to be considered, the applicant must be, or have been, the licensee in the state of Colorado. DIRECTOR QUALIFICATIONS - SMALL CHILD CARE CENTER (up to 15 children) The director or substitute director of a small center must either: meet large center director qualifications or meet at least one of the following qualifications: Possess a current teaching license issued by the Colorado Department of Education with an endorsement in the area of elementary education, early childhood education, early childhood special education, early childhood special education specialist; or principal licensure; Possess a current early childhood professional credential level II or higher in version 3.0 as determined by the Department; Current certification as a child development associate (CDA) credential in: center- based, preschool; center-based, infant-toddler; or family child care; or other Department-approved credential; Two years and nine months (5,005 hours) of satisfactory experience in the care and supervision of four or more children less than eight years of age who are not related to the individual, and at least two three-semester credit hour courses from an accredited college or university in early childhood education, and one of the courses must be either: a. Introduction to Early Childhood; or b. Early Childhood Guidance Strategies for Children or has been issued Colorado Pyramid Model Training certificate of completion Nine months (1,365 hours) of satisfactory experience in the care and supervision of four or more children less than eight years of age who are not related to the individual, and an Associate’s degree from an accredited college or university, with at least two three-semester credit hour courses in early childhood education, and one of the courses must be either: a. Introduction to Early Childhood Professions; or b. Early Childhood Guidance Strategies for children or has been issued a Colorado Pyramid Model Training certificate of completion. 6) Three months (455 hours) of satisfactory experience in the care and supervision of four or more children less than eight years of age who are not related to the individual; and an Associate’s degree in child development or early childhood education from an accredited college or university, with at least two three-semester credit hour courses in either: a. Introduction to Early Childhood Professions or possesses a Child Development Associate (CDA) credential in: Center-Based, Preschool; Center-Based, Infant- Toddler; or Family Child Care; or b. Early Childhood Guidance Strategies for Children or has been issued a Colorado Pyramid Model Training certificate of completion. DIRECTOR QUALIFICATIONS- SCHOOL-AGE CHILD CARE CENTER A. Program Director 1. Each program must have an on-site director. The director is responsible for operating the center in accordance with licensing rules, planning, and implementing the program as well as the supervision of staff. 2. The program director must be at least twenty-one (21) years of age, and must have completed at least one (1) the following qualifications: a. A Bachelor’s, Master’s, or Doctorate degree from an accredited college or university with a major area of study in one (1) of the following areas: 1. Child Development 2. Psychology 3. Early Childhood Education 4. Early Childhood Special Education 5. Elementary Education 6. Elementary Special Education 7. Family and Human Development 8. Family Studies 9. Special Education 10. Outdoor Education 11. Recreation 12. Human Services b. An associate’s degree or sixty (60) semester credit hours from an accredited college or university and three (3) months (455 hours) of experience in the care and supervision of four (4) or more children over the ages of four (4) years who are not related to the individual; or c. Twenty-one (21) months (3,185 hours) of experience in the care and supervision of four (4) or more children over the ages of four (4) years who are not related to the individual and one of the following qualifications: 1. Completion of six (6) semester hours, from a regionally accredited college or university; or 2. Completion of forty (40) clock hours of training in coursework applicable to school-age children within the first nine months in the director position. The 40 clock hours of training cannot include any of the required trainings as listed in rule section 2.508. d. A current early childhood professional credential level II (2) or higher in version 3.0 as determined by the Department. b. Licensed family child care Describe the provider qualifications for licensed family child care homes, including any variations based on the ages of children in care: Colorado has variations of provider qualifications based on the ages of children in care. Providers serving more infants and toddlers need additional training, as outlined below. All Providers and/or equally qualified substitutes must be at least 18 years of age. Aides must be at least 16 years of age. Aides and volunteers must work under the direct supervision of a primary provider or equally qualified substitute at all times. Primary providers and equally qualified substitutes, regardless of the type of family child care home, must complete the following training: 15 hours of pre-licensing training, pediatric CPR and First Aid Certification, Standard Precautions, Medication Administration, Safe Sleep, Building and Physical Premises Safety, Immunizations, Shaken Baby Abusive Head Trauma, and Child Abuse Prevention. The primary provider must be the resident of the home. A ￿Large Family Child Care Home￿ provider or equally qualified substitute must meet one of the following criteria: 1) A minimum of 21 months of documented satisfactory experience in the group care of children under the age of six years or as a licensed family child care home in Colorado. Equal experience operating as an approved military child care home is accepted. 2) A minimum of 60 credit hours of college education from a regionally accredited college or university, with at least one college course in early childhood education, plus one year of documented satisfactory experience in the group care of children as: A licensed family child care home in Colorado; A military licensed family child care home; A Colorado certified family foster home; or A staff member in a licensed child care center. 3) Current certification as a child development associate (CDA). 4) Completion of CDEC-approved Expanding Quality in Infant/Toddler care course or three semester credit hours from a regionally accredited college or university in infant/toddler theory prior to licensing: a. A minimum of one year (1,820 hours) of experience as a licensed child care provider holding a permanent license in Colorado immediately before becoming a licensee of a large child care home An ￿infant toddler family child care home￿ provider or equally qualified substitute must also meet one of the following criteria: 1) Must have completed the Department approved Expanding Quality in Infant/Toddler care course or three semester hours from a regionally accredited college or university in infant/toddler theory prior to licensing: a. A minimum of one year (1,820 hours) of full time experience in a licensed program caring for children who are younger than three years old. 2) Must have completed CDEC-approved Expanding Quality in Infant/Toddler care course or three semester credit hours from a regionally accredited college or university in infant/toddler theory prior to licensing: a. A current Early Childhood Professional credential level 3 or higher in version 3.0as determined by the Department based on its Early Childhood Professional Credential 3.0 Worksheet, found at https://drive.google.com/file/d/10FQQw4q0G01W9Ssczs0o1Kkit2HhkbFV/view, or a current director qualifications letter issued by the Department. The ￿Three Under 18 Months Family Child Care Home￿ provider or equally qualified substitute must also have completed the Department approved Expanding Quality in Infant/Toddler care course or three semester credit hours from a regionally accredited college or university in infant/toddler theory prior to licensing The ￿experienced family child care provider license￿ provider or equally qualified substitute must also: 1) Have been a licensed family child care home in Colorado for at least the last five consecutive years; have equal experience operating as a licensed military family child care home is acceptable; or 9,100 hours of documented experience working in a Colorado licensed child care facility in the role as a director or as a Department certified early childhood teacher based on the qualifications found at https://cdec.colorado.gov/professional-certifications; 2) Have completed the department-approved Expanding Quality in Infant/Toddler care course, or three semester credit hours from a regionally accredited college or university in infant/toddler theory; 3) Have completed 75 clock hours of training within the preceding five years, or have a current early childhood professional credential level III or higher as determined by the Department using version 3.0 of its worksheet found at https://drive.google.com/file/d/10FQQw4q0G01W9Ssczs0o1Kkit2HhkbFV/view; or individuals who have a current director qualifications letter issued by the Department. The 75 clock hours of training does not include pre-licensing training, standard precautions, First Aid and CPR, or Medication Administration training. c. Licensed, regulated, or registered in-home care (care in the child’s own home by a non- relative) Describe the provider qualifications for licensed, regulated, or registered in-home care providers (care in the child’s own home) including any variations based on the ages of children in care: Colorado does not regulate care in the child's own home in cases where the number of children served is below statutory exemption requirements. If the number of children in care exceeds exemption limits, they are required to obtain a family child care license. 5.2.4 Teacher/caregiver qualifications for license-exempt providers Provide the teacher/provider qualification requirements (for instance, age, high school diploma, specific training, etc.) for the license-exempt providers under the following categories of care: a. License-exempt center-based child care. N/A b. License-exempt home-based child care. Qualified Exempt Providers must be at least 18 years of age, shall not be the adult caretaker or teen parent of the child that is receiving care, and shall not be a sibling of the child that is receiving care if living in the same residence. They are required to complete 15 hours of pre-service training, including: Emergency and Disaster Preparedness for Child Care Providers; How Experiences Impact Early Brain Development (1st year)/child development course (consecutive years); Injury Prevention for Child Care Homes ; Introduction to First Aid and CPR; Part 1: Medication Administration Training (MAT); Playground Safety for Homes; Preventing Shaken Baby Syndrome and Abusive Head Trauma; Infant Safe Sleep Practices; Recognition and Reporting of Child Abuse an Neglect; Standard Precautions, including Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases and Immunizations; Transportation Rules; CCCAP Provider Basics Course. Qualified Exempt providers also must complete an Emergency Plan and Fire Safety. Building and Physical Premises is included in training. c. License-exempt in-home care (care in the child’s own home). Qualified Exempt Providers must be at least 18 years of age, shall not be the adult caretaker or teen parent of the child that is receiving care, and shall not be a sibling of the child that is receiving care if living in the same residence. All non-relative qualified exempt providers are required to complete 15 hours of pre-service training, including: Emergency and Disaster Preparedness for Child Care Providers; How Experiences Impact Early Brain Development (1st year)/child development course (consecutive years); Injury Prevention for Child Care Homes ; Introduction to First Aid and CPR; Part 1: Medication Administration Training (MAT); Playground Safety for Homes; Preventing Shaken Baby Syndrome and Abusive Head Trauma; Infant Safe Sleep Practices; Recognition and Reporting of Child Abuse an Neglect; Standard Precautions, including Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases and Immunizations; Transportation Rules; CCCAP Provider Basics Course. Qualified Exempt providers also must complete an Emergency Plan and Fire Safety. Building and Physical Premises is included in training. Additionally, in order to ensure the safety of children in care, CDEC requires all legally exempt non-relative providers, who provide child care in their homes or the homes of children, annually complete ten (10) core areas of required trainings.

body: Lead Agencies must have health and safety standards for providers serving children receiving CCDF assistance relating to the required health and safety topics as appropriate to the provider setting and age of the children served. This requirement is applicable to all child care programs receiving CCDF funds regardless of licensing status (i.e., licensed or license-exempt). The only exception to this requirement is for relative providers, as defined by CCDF. Lead Agencies have the option of exempting certain relatives from any or all CCDF health and safety requirements. Exemptions for relative providers’ standards requirements will be addressed in question 5.8.1. Describe the following health and safety standards for programs serving children receiving CCDF assistance on the following topics (note that monitoring and enforcement will be addressed in subsection 5.5): 5.3.1 Prevention and control of infectious diseases (including immunizations) health and safety standard a. Provide the standards, appropriate to the provider setting and age of children, that address the prevention and control of infectious diseases for the following CCDF-eligible providers: i. All CCDF-eligible licensed center care. Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration, includes in the child care licensing standards requirements on the prevention and control of infectious disease (including immunizations). These requirements include Immunization training requirements for staff and CDEC-approved child care health consultants responsible for the collection, review, and maintenance of child immunization records. Standard precautions training requirement for all staff. Parents must provide documentation of school- required immunization status or certificate of medical or nonmedical exemption for children at the time of enrollment. The procedure concerning admission and registration of children including whether non-immunized or under-immunized children are enrolled in the program. Staff members must be current for all immunizations required by their employer, physical premises, and health and safety requirements. In addition, Child Care Centers must document compliance with the CDPHE rules and regulations governing the health and sanitation of child care facilities. The "Rules And Regulations Governing The Health And Sanitation Of Child Care Facilities In The State Of Colorado" 6 CCR 1010-7 can be found at 6 CCR 1010-7 . These rules govern the minimum health and sanitation requirements for the operation and maintenance of child care facilities to protect the health of children and staff in these facilities. Content Covered in this set of the rules include: Premises, Facility, Sanitary Facilities and Controls, Interior Design, Disease Prevention, Food Service, Infant and Toddler Programs and as Applicable to Older Children, Care of Animals, Toxic Materials Management, and,Compliance Procedures. ii. All CCDF-eligible licensed family child care homes. Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration, includes in the family child care home licensing standards requirements on the prevention and control of infectious disease (including immunizations). These requirements include Immunization training requirements for staff responsible for the collection, review, and maintenance of child immunization records. Standard precautions training requirement for all staff. Parents must provide documentation of school-required immunization status or certificate of medical or nonmedical exemption for children at the time of enrollment. The procedure concerning admission and registration of children including whether non-immunized or under-immunized children are enrolled in the program. Staff members must be current for all immunizations required by their employer, physical premises, and health and safety requirements. iii. All CCDF-eligible licensed in-home care. Provide the standard: N/A [x] Not applicable. iv. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt center care. Provide the standard: N/A v. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt family child care homes. Provide the standard: Qualified Exempt Child Care Providers that are providing care for a child they are not related to must complete all assigned pre-service health and safety training approved by the state department of early childhood, within three months of providing services as a Qualified Exempt child care provider. 3.127 (B)(7)(a) 8 CCR 1403-1. The assigned training requirements include Immunization training requirements for Qualified Exempt Child Care Providers on the prevention and control of infectious disease (including immunizations). Qualified Exempt non-relative providers are notified of their training requirements and implement the content of the training through their orientation call, their health and safety inspection precall and visit, the self-assurance form (signed by provider) and their fiscal agreement (signed by provider). vi. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt in-home care. Provide the standard: Qualified Exempt Child Care Providers that are providing care for a child they are not related to must complete all assigned pre-service health and safety training approved by the state department of early childhood, within three months of providing services as a Qualified Exempt child care provider. 3.127 (B)(7)(a) 8 CCR 1403-1. The assigned training requirements include Immunization training requirements for Qualified Exempt Child Care Providers on the prevention and control of infectious disease (including immunizations). Qualified Exempt non-relative providers are notified of their training requirements and implementing the content of the training through their orientation call, their health and safety inspection precall and visit, the self-assurance form (signed by provider, and their fiscal agreement (signed by provider). vii. All CCDF-eligible out-of-school programs (afterschool programs, summer camps, day camps, etc.). Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration, include in the school-age child care licensing standards requirements on the prevention and control of infectious disease (including immunizations). These requirements include Immunization training requirements for staff responsible for the collection, review, and maintenance of child immunization records. Standard precautions training requirement for all staff. Parents must provide documentation of school-required immunization status or certificate of medical or nonmedical exemption for children at the time of enrollment. The procedure concerning admission and registration of children including whether non-immunized or under-immunized children are enrolled in the program. Staff members must be current for all immunizations required by their employer, physical premises, and health and safety requirements. In addition, School-Age Child Care Centers must document compliance with the CDPHE rules and regulations governing the health and sanitation of child care facilities. These rules govern the minimum health and sanitation requirements for the operation and maintenance of child care facilities in order to protect the health of children and staff in these facilities. Content Covered in this set of the rule include, Premises, Facility, Sanitary Facilities and Controls, Interior Design, Disease Prevention, Food Service, Infant and Toddler Programs and as Applicable to Older Children, Care of Animals, Toxic Materials Management, and Compliance Procedures. b. Provide the standards, appropriate to the provider setting and age of children, that address that children attending child care programs under CCDF are age-appropriately immunized, according to the latest recommendation for childhood immunizations of the respective State public health agency, for the following CCDF-eligible providers: i. All CCDF-eligible licensed center care. All CCDF-eligible licensed family child care homes. Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration includes in the family child care licensing standards Immunization. At the time of admission, the parent or guardian must provide the following information to the provider for each child entering the family child care home documentation of school-required immunization status or certificate of medical or nonmedical exemption, is required by the Colorado Board of Health. Up-to-date school-required immunizations must be documented as specified on the CDPHE certificate of immunization or on an ￿approved alternate￿ Certificate of Immunization, defined in Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment rules located in 6 CCR 1009-2 rule section CCR 1402-1. iii. All CCDF-eligible licensed in-home care. Provide the standard: [x] Not applicable. iv. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt center care. Provide the standard: N/A v. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt family child care homes. Provide the standard: Counties shall obtain verification immunization record to the county, indicating that the children are age-appropriately immunized or have a religious or medical exemption (see sections 25-4902 and 25-4-908, C.R.S., for exemption requirements) for children who receive child care from Qualified Exempt child care providers not related to the child(ren), where care is provided outside of the child’s home, and the child(ren) are not school age at application and re- determination. 3.125 (T) 8 CCR 1403-1. vi. All CCDF-eligible license-exempt in-home care. Provide the standard: Counties shall obtain verification immunization records to the county, indicating that the children are age-appropriately immunized or have a religious or medical exemption (see sections 25-4902 and 25-4-908, C.R.S., for exemption requirements) for children who receive child care from Qualified Exempt child care providers not related to the child(ren), where care is provided outside of the child’s home, and the child(ren) are not school age at application and re- determination. 3.125 (T) 8 CCR 1403-1. vii. All CCDF-eligible out-of-school programs (afterschool programs, summer camps, day camps, etc.). Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration, includes in the school-age child care licensing standards Immunization requirements. Specifically, at the time of enrollment, the parent(s)/ guardian(s) must provide for each child entering Documentation of school- required immunization status or Certificate of Medical or Nonmedical Exemption, required by the Colorado Board of Health. Up-to-date school-required immunizations must be documented as specified on the CDPHE Certificate of Immunization or on an ￿approved alternate '' Certificate of Immunization, defined in Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment regulation at 6 CCR. 5.3.2 Prevention of sudden infant death syndrome and the use of safe-sleep practices health and safety standard Provide the standards, appropriate to the provider setting and age of children, that address the prevention of sudden infant death syndrome and use of safe sleeping practices for the following CCDF-eligible providers: i. All CCDF-eligible licensed center care. Provide the standard: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration includes requirements within the child care licensing standards for the prevention of sudden infant death syndrome and the use of safe sleep practices. Included safe sleep standards: Staff working with infants less than twelve (12) months old must complete a Department- approved safe sleep training prior to working with infants less than twelve (12) months old. This training must be renewed annually and will be counted towards ongoing professional development. Staff working with infants less than twelve (12) months old must complete a Department-approved safe sleep training prior to working with infants less than twelve (12) months old. This training must be renewed annually and will be counted towards ongoing professional development. The written policies and procedures must be developed, implemented, and followed, and must include at a minimum the following information: The procedure for establishing safe sleep environments for infants includes how staff will supervise and physically check on infants who are sleeping. Standards for Safe Sleep Environments for Infants: 1. Each infant up to eighteen (18) months of age and enrolled in the infant program must be provided with an individual crib, futon approved for infants, or other approved sleep/rest equipment meeting Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards published by the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) at 16 CFR section 1218.2 (April 23, 2015); 16 CFR section 1219.2 (October 28, 2019); 16 CFR section 1220.2 (June 3, 2023); 16 CFR section 1221.2 (January 20, 2020); 16 CFR section 1222.2 (August 5, 2023); 16 C.F.R. section 1236.2 (June 23, 2022); and 16 C.F.R 1241.2 (February 15, 2022) herein incorporated by reference. No later editions or amendments are incorporated. These regulations are available at no cost from the CPSC at https://www.ecfr.gov. These regulations are also available for public inspection and copying at the Colorado Department of Early Childhood, 710 S. Ash St., Bldg. C, Denver, CO 80246, during regular business hours. Individual cribs or futons must provide each infant with sufficient space for the infant’s length, size, and movement. 2. In the infant room, soft bedding or materials that could pose a suffocation hazard are not permitted in cribs, futons approved for infants, or other approved sleep/rest equipment. Soft bedding means, but is not limited to, any soft sleep surface like bumper pads, pillows, blankets, quilts, comforters, sleep positioning devices, sheepskins, blankets, flat sheets, cloth diaper bibs, plush toys, pacifiers with stuffed animals attached, and stuffed animals. a. Mattresses for cribs and futons must have a properly fitted, clean sheet. 3. body: Lead Agencies must have requirements for all caregivers, teachers, and directors at CCDF providers to complete pre-service or orientation training (within 3 months of starting) on all CCDF health and safety standards and child development. The training must be appropriate to the setting and the age of children served. This training must address the required health and safety standards and the content area of child development. Lead Agencies have flexibility in determining the minimum number of training hours to require, and are encouraged to consult with Caring for our Children Basics for best practices. Exemptions for relative providers’ training requirements are addressed in question 5.8.1. 5.4.1 Health and safety pre-service/orientation training requirements Lead Agencies must certify staff have pre-service or orientation training on each standard that is appropriate to different settings and age groups. Lead Agencies may require pre-service or orientation to be completed before staff can care for children unsupervised. In the table below, check the boxes for which you have training requirements. -- Is this standard addressed in the pre-service or orientation training? Is the pre-service or orientation training on this standard appropriate to different settings and age groups? Does the Lead Agency require staff to complete the training before caring for children unsupervised? a. Prevention and control of infectious diseases (including immunizations) [x] [x] [x] b. SIDS prevention and use of safe sleep practices [x] [x] [x] c. Administration of medication [x] [x] [x] d. Prevention and response to food and allergic reactions [x] [x] [x] e. Building and physical premises safety, including identification of and protection from hazards, bodies of water, and vehicular traffic [x] [x] [x] f. Prevention of shaken baby syndrome, abusive head trauma and child maltreatment [x] [x] [x] m. If the Lead Agency does not certify implementation of all the health and safety pre- service/orientation training requirements for staff in programs serving children receiving CCDF assistance, please describe: Colorado currently requires that all Family Child Care Home providers have current First Aid and CPR certification, infant and toddler programs have at least one person who holds current First Aid and CPR certification in the infant and toddler program classrooms at all times, and there must be at least one staff member for every 30 or fewer children with current First Aid and CPR certification present at all times for preschool and school-age children. Current CPR and First Aid certification is also required for anyone transporting children. Colorado has successfully implemented these rules for over two decades to protect the health, safety, and well-being of children in care. The Department created a free online module as an introduction to basic first aid, what to do for children in an emergency, and how to get CPR certified. This training is required for staff working in family child care homes, child care centers, and school-age programs who are not required to be certified in First Aid and CPR and must be renewed every two years. It is also a required training for CCCAP Qualified Exempt (QE) providers and must be renewed annually. Colorado has had these requirements in place since 2017 and has previously been monitored and found to be in compliance. Colorado believed we remained in compliance with the CPR requirement. Colorado is adding the steps to perform CPR to the Department-approved Introduction to First Aid and CPR module.
