body: 6.3.1 Required hours of ongoing training Provide the number of hours of ongoing training required annually for CCDF-eligible providers in the following settings: a. Licensed child care centers: CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration requires through licensing rules that all licensed providers receive 15 hours of annual ongoing training, including at least 3 hours in social-emotional training. b. License-exempt child care centers: N/A c. Licensed family child care homes: The Colorado Department of Early Childhood, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration requires through licensing rules that all licensed providers, including licensed family child care homes, receive 15 hours of annual ongoing training, including at least 3 hours in social-emotional training. d. License-exempt family child care homes: The Colorado Department of Early Childhood, Division of Child Care Assistance requires through CCCAP rules that all Qualified Exempt non-relative providers receive 15 hours of annual ongoing training. e. Regulated or registered in-home child care: N/A f. Non-regulated or registered in-home child care: Non-relative Qualified Exempt Providers providing care under the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program (CCCAP) complete the following training annually: Emergency and Disaster Preparedness for Child Care Providers, How Experiences Impact Early Brain Development (Year 1); Infant Safe Sleep Practices; Injury Prevention for Homes; Introduction to First Aid and CPR; Medication Administration Training; Playground Safety for Homes; Preventing Shaken Baby Syndrome and Abusive Head Trauma; Recognition and Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect; Standard Precautions, including Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases and Immunization; CCCAP Provider Basics Course; Transportation Rules; a child development course of their choosing (Year 2). All training is Department approved and completed in CDEC Professional Development Information System. 6.3.2 Accessibility of professional development for Tribal organizations Describe how the Lead Agency’s training and professional development are accessible to providers supported through Indian tribes or Tribal organizations receiving CCDF funds (as applicable). The Colorado Shines PDIS contains a Learning Management System that makes training widely available. As training is approved and added to the system - including training required by licensing as well as ongoing professional development - the self paced e-learning modules are available to professionals across the state. In addition, many of the modules are available as face- to-face learning experiences and can be utilized by qualified trainers statewide, including trainers associated with Indian tribes and tribal organizations. 6.3.3 Professional development appropriate for the diversity of children, families, and child care providers Describe how the Lead Agency’s training and professional development requirements reflect the diversity of children, families, and child care providers participating in CCDF. To the extent practicable, how does professional development include specialized training or credentials for providers who care for infants or school-age children; individuals with limited English proficiency; children who are bilingual; children with developmental delays or disabilities; and/or Native Americans, including Indians, as the term is defined in Section 900.6 in subpart B of the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (including Alaska Natives) and Native Hawaiians? CDEC, Division of Early Learning Licensing and Administration (DELLA), requires coursework that is developed for child care providers and is aligned with the Colorado Competencies for Early Childhood Educators and Administrators. The content areas of these competencies, otherwise known as domains, describe knowledge and skills that early childhood educators need in order to work effectively with children from birth through age eight and their families. To increase knowledge and skills, early childhood educators are expected to participate in quality continuing education opportunities (e.g., college classes, community-based training, etc.). The domains included within Colorado’s Competencies for Early Childhood Educators and Administrators are: child growth, development, and learning; child observation and assessment; family and community partnerships; social-emotional health and development promotion; health, safety, and nutrition; professional practice; and teaching practices. DELLA requires through regulation that all licensed providers and staff complete the Department-approved trainings: ￿Recognizing the Impact of Bias on Early Childhood Professionals￿ or other Department-approved training on implicit bias, ￿Working with an Early Childhood Mental Health Consultant,￿ and ￿Introduction to the Early Intervention and Preschool Special Education Programs.￿ For school-age programs, DELLA requires through regulation that all licensed providers complete ￿Injury Prevention￿ and ￿Playground Safety for School-Age Child Care Centers￿ to address the unique safety concerns of school-age programs. Providers who care for infants and toddlers have a variety of ongoing professional development available, in addition to their required training. This includes the ￿Infant and Toddler Care Sequence,￿ a six-hour free, online course sequence that focuses on the six practices that are essential in infant and toddler group care settings and the ￿Expanding Quality in Infant Toddler Care (EQIT) Course,￿ a 45-hour instructor-led training. Supporting the diverse workforce is also a priority for the Department. For example, Spanish is the second most spoken language in Colorado. The Colorado Shines Professional Development Information System (PDIS) and its coursework are available in Spanish. In addition, CDEC is in the process of translating its required coursework into Arabic. In addition to required training, CDEC offers a growing number of instructor-led and online, self-paced eLearning courses in Spanish for individuals to meet licensing requirements and engage in ongoing professional development related to Colorado Shines or other related topics in the field. Evaluation data is collected to assess the ongoing need to offer a more broad range of professional content in Spanish or other non-English languages. All participant-facing materials associated with the Expanding Quality in Infant Toddler Care (EQIT) Course are translated into and maintained in Spanish. Expanding Quality Infant Toddler Specialists are able to provide the EQIT course in Spanish and Arabic. Finally, the Early Childhood Competency Self-Assessment is translated into Spanish. The competencies outline what an individual should know and be able to do based on their role. CDEC also offers training to support children who are bilingual. Specifically, Module 8 of the Language and Literacy sequence focuses on young dual/English language learners. CDEC has also connected with external training providers to offer the instructor-led training ￿Dual Language Learners: Stages of Second Language Development and the Impact on Learning.￿ 6.3.4 Child developmental screening Describe how all providers receive, through training and professional development, information about: (1) existing resources and services the State/Territory can make available in conducting developmental screenings and providing referrals to services when appropriate for children who receive assistance under this part, including the coordinated use of the Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment program (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.) and developmental screening services available under section 619 and part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (20 U.S.C. 1419, 1431 et seq.); and (2) how child care providers may utilize these resources and services to obtain developmental screenings for children who receive assistance and who may be at risk for cognitive or other developmental delays, which may include social, emotional, physical, or linguistic delays: DELLA requires, through regulation, that all licensed providers and staff complete the Introduction to the Early Intervention and Preschool Special Education Programs course, which is available for free to all professionals through the PDIS. The training covers introductory competencies related to child development, growth, and learning. Providers can use the resources in the training to develop responsive and inclusive referral procedures and family engagement practices.

body: Lead Agencies must develop, maintain, or implement early learning and developmental guidelines appropriate for children from birth to kindergarten entry. Early learning and developmental guidelines should describe what children should know and be able to do at different ages and cover the essential domains of early childhood development, which at a minimum includes cognition, including language arts and mathematics; social, emotional, and physical development; and approaches toward learning. 6.4.1 Early learning and developmental guidelines a. Check the boxes below to certify the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines are: i. [x] Research-based. ii. [x] Developmentally appropriate. iii. [x] Culturally and linguistically appropriate. iv. [x] Aligned with kindergarten entry. v. [x] Appropriate for all children from birth to kindergarten entry. vi. [x] Implemented in consultation with the educational agency and the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care or similar coordinating body. vii. If any components above are not checked, describe: b. Check the boxes below to certify that the required domains are included in the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines. i. [x] Cognition, including language arts and mathematics. ii. [x] Social development. iii. [x] Emotional development. iv. [x] Physical development. v. [x] Approaches toward learning. vi. [x] Other optional domains. Describe any optional domains: The Guidelines address the following content areas for children ages three to five: 1) social studies knowledge and skills and 2) creative arts expression. Additional content areas addressed for children kindergarten through third grade: music, dance, visual arts, drama and theater arts. Transition supports are also addressed for the following: 1) transition to home; 2) infancy to toddlerhood; 3) home to school; 4) early intervention (Part C) to preschool special education (Part B); and 5) transition to kindergarten. vii. If any components above are not checked, describe: c. When were the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines most recently updated and for what reason? The Colorado Early Learning and Development Guidelines (https://earlylearningco.org/) were originally developed and endorsed by the Colorado Early Childhood Leadership Commission in 2011. They were updated in 2019 as one of the five required activities under the Colorado Preschool Development Grant, and specifically designed to maximize parental choice and knowledge. As part of this update, the Guidelines were aligned with the 2020 Colorado Academic Standards and the 2015 Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework (HSELOF). Throughout the update process, stakeholders from a wide variety of agencies and sectors were involved, including representatives from the Colorado Department of Education, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, the Colorado Department of Human Services, Head Start, local child care providers, higher education, early learning professionals, and others. An Advisory Board met numerous times to ensure the resulting guidelines reflect a strong research base, enhance working early childhood systems in Colorado, and meet the needs of diverse audiences and purposes. The Guidelines were reviewed and advised by state experts with knowledge of early childhood development and teaching practice, as well as specific content areas. The most recent update of the Guidelines was finalized in May 2019, and they are updated at least every 10 years. d. Provide the Web link to the Lead Agency's early learning and developmental guidelines. https://earlylearningco.org/ 6.4.2 Use of early learning and developmental guidelines a. Describe how the Lead Agency uses its early learning and developmental guidelines. Colorado’s Early Learning and Development Guidelines (ELDGs) are used statewide by child care providers and in the development and implementation of training and professional development. There are required alignments to the ELDGs included within the state's QRIS related to curriculum and child assessment. The PDIS offers a course specifically on the ELDGs, and serves as a primary opportunity for members of the early childhood workforce to meet a training requirement regarding child development. Through Preschool Development Grant (PDG) B-5 funding, Colorado developed family- friendly videos and a digital marketing campaign for the ELDGs. CDEC utilizes digital marketing to promote the ELDGs ongoing. Additionally, print versions of the ELDGs in English and Spanish are distributed to families, local Early Childhood Councils, Family Resource Centers, and during conferences and events. There is ongoing promotion of the website and videos including through Bright by Text. Additionally, the ELDGs were utilized as the basis for the PLAYbooks, a resource that supports parents and caregivers in understanding and promoting their child’s development through everyday activities. Finally, the ELDGs were rewritten into plain language and embedded in the forthcoming Raising CO Kids Guide website to make them even more accessible to families. b. Check the boxes below to certify that CCDF funds are not used to develop or implement an assessment for children that: i. [x] Will be the primary or sole basis to determine a child care provider ineligible to participate in the CCDF. ii. [x] Will be used as the primary or sole basis to provide a reward or sanction for an individual provider. iii. [x] Will be used as the primary or sole method for assessing program effectiveness. iv. [x] Will be used to deny children eligibility to participate in CCDF. v. If any components above are not checked, describe: 7 Quality Improvement Activities The quality of child care directly affects children’s safety and healthy development while in care settings, and high-quality child care can be foundational across the lifespan. Lead Agencies may use CCDF for quality improvement activities for all children in care, not just those receiving child care subsidies. OCC will collect the most detailed Lead Agency information about quality improvement activities in annual reports instead of this Plan. Lead Agencies must report on CCDF child care quality improvement investments in three ways: 1. In this Plan, Lead Agencies will describe the types of activities supported by quality investments over the 3-year period. 2. An annual expenditure report (the ACF-696). Lead Agencies will provide data on how much CCDF funding is spent on quality activities. This report will be used to determine compliance with the required quality and infant and toddler spending requirements. 3. An annual Quality Progress Report (the ACF-218). Lead Agencies will provide a description of activities funded by quality expenditures, the measures used to evaluate its progress in improving the quality of child care programs and services within the State/Territory, and progress or barriers encountered on those measures. In this section of the Plan, Lead Agencies will describe their quality activities needs assessment and identify the types of quality improvement activities where CCDF investments are being made using quality set-aside funds.

body: 7.1.1 Needs assessment process and findings a. Describe the Lead Agency needs assessment process for expending CCDF funds on activities to improve the quality of child care, including the frequency of assessment, how a diverse range of parents and providers were consulted, and how their views are incorporated: Colorado utilizes a range of strategies to assess needs, including utilizing data to inform data-driven decision making and engaging parents and providers. Colorado implements Colorado Shines, a statewide Tiered Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS), to ensure children receive the highest quality programming in all licensed settings serving children prior to kindergarten entry (https://decl.my.salesforce-sites.com/programs?p=Overview-of-the-ratings-process). The Colorado Shines QRIS (https://decl.my.salesforce-sites.com/programs?p=Overview-of-the- ratings-process) includes integrated technology systems, which provide an opportunity to develop and track data-informed goals for quality improvement: -The Colorado Shines Professional Development and Information System (https://www.coloradoshinespdis.com/s/pdislogin?language=en_US) and the Colorado Shines QRIS technology system are integrated to share data related to employee professional development and credentials, which inform the progression and point accumulation for child care programs within the Workforce and Professional Development quality standard. -Integration with the State Child Care Licensing System enables Colorado Shines to always have up-to-date program license data and basic program profile information. -The data exchange between the Quality Improvement Grant Management System enables the program to see what funding is available, as well as the ability to apply for quality improvement grants. -Finally, including child care resource and referral (https://decl.my.salesforce- sites.com//search) functionality within the Colorado Shines website enables referral specialists to easily help families search for programs that match their needs and criteria with ease and in turn provide a better experience for families and their children. CDEC utilizes data from the Colorado Shines technology system and linked state databases to 1) support and sustain increased program quality across the state; 2) evaluate the progress of both professionals and programs; 3) assess and inform the presence of quality and areas of need; and 4) inform how quality investments are made and accessible to the highest number of programs to support quality improvement. CDEC develops goals through a performance-based analysis strategy that allows every program to focus on and improve performance outcomes. Through this process, CDEC is able to make more informed, collaborative decisions to align efforts and resources to affect positive change. There are a number of early childhood goals tracked through the Governor’s Dashboard (https://dashboard.colorado.gov/), which provides a summary of how Colorado is progressing on the Governor’s vision. These processes allow for the tracking of goals and continuous quality improvement efforts through: the collection of timely data; increasing transparency; conducting regular executive and cabinet meetings to assess the effectiveness of the strategies; and identifying new performance measures. CDEC collects data for analytic purposes to identify positive trends and opportunities for improvement. When improvements are needed, CDEC determines and implements appropriate strategies. CDEC Family Voice Council (FVC) is a diverse group of parents and caregivers who provide guidance on programs, services and supports across the early childhood system. Working with the FVC has resulted in more family-friendly materials (such as the CCCAP application, which the FVC reviewed); guidance and prioritization on grants and plans developed by CDEC; and a stronger commitment to equity across the Department’s work. CDEC recently completed an updated Statewide Early Childhood Needs Assessment in 2023 utilizing funding from the Preschool Development Grant Birth through Five. The assessment was guided by the CDEC Family Voice Council throughout the process, and families were further engaged through focus groups available in English and Spanish. In addition to the qualitative data, the assessment also relied on a wealth of existing data from programs and research conducted over the last few years, including CDEC family surveys. The Needs Assessment explored the following questions with regard to quality: 1. How good are Colorado’s early childhood programs? Do different types of families have the same access to high-quality programs? 2. What gets in the way of providing top-quality programs? What are some ideas for solving these problems? Findings related to these questions included the following: 1. In addition to school readiness, early childhood services should emphasize a whole-child approach. 2. Early childhood programs have an opportunity to think broadly about what they mean by quality improvement. 3. About half of early child care and education providers have not advanced their Colorado Shines rating beyond a Level 1. 4. Families say quality is important, but they do not use quality ratings to make decisions about child care. CDEC staff are considering these findings in their work and sharing them across the state with partners b. Describe the findings of the assessment, including any findings related to needs of different populations and types of providers, and if any overarching goals for quality improvement were identified: Colorado includes multiple components that make up the overarching goals to improve the quality of child care services: quality standards (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c7xCyiti7zJOE_ORzb3mDAjHf2dKdsJ8/view), improvement supports, quality incentives, and support for implementation. Quality standards include child care licensing regulations and quality indicators outlined within the Colorado Shines Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS). Colorado Shines includes five standard areas that research has shown are related to program quality: Child Health; Family Partnerships; Leadership Management and Administration; Learning Environment; and, Workforce and Professional Development. In addition to accumulating the total number of points required for each rating Levels 3-5, programs must meet points in all 5 standard areas as well as minimum levels of quality as measured by the appropriate Early Childhood Environment Rating Scale (ERS). To support quality improvement, Colorado Offers programs for professional development and coaching to support best practices. Quality Incentives are offered statewide to support quality improvement. Finally, support for implementation includes funding to support the recruitment and engagement of programs, training and supervision for technical assistance staff, and data systems development, integration and maintenance. These goals were selected as priorities for CDEC in partnership with the ECLC, Colorado's State Advisory Council.

body: Lead Agencies must use a portion of their CCDF expenditures for activities designed to improve the quality of child care services and to increase parental options for and access to high-quality child care. They must use the quality set-aside funds on at least one of 10 activities described in CCDF and the quality activities must be aligned with a Statewide or Territory-wide assessment of the State's or Territory’s need to carry out such services and care. 7.2.1 Quality improvement activities a. Describe how the Lead Agency will make its Quality Progress Report (ACF – 218) and expenditure reports, available to the public. Provide a link if available. This information is available upon request. We regularly update partners on quality initiatives and investments through ECLC and its subcommittees as well as advisory groups and committees across CDEC. CDEC posts its State Plan at https://cdec.colorado.gov/resources/state-plans. b. Identify Lead Agency plans, if any, to spend CCDF funds for each of the following quality improvement activities. If an activity is checked “yes”, describe the Lead Agency’s current and/or future plans for this activity. i. Supporting the training and professional development of the child care workforce, including birth to five and school-age providers. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. CDEC’s efforts to support the training and professional development of the child care workforce are grounded in the strategic goal to recruit, support and retain highly competent, caring and diverse early childhood professionals across early childhood care and education settings serving children and families. To achieve this goal, current and future activities include: 1) promoting systemic and structural opportunities to increase funding for compensation and benefits and other mechanisms that support the economic, social and mental well being of the early childhood workforce; 2) creating aligned and accessible credential and qualification pathways to foster a comprehensive early childhood professional workforce that reflects the children and families of Colorado communities; 3) providing training, mentoring, coaching and consultative opportunities for the early childhood workforce to identify and build on their unique strengths and skills and to engage in reflective practices that support their ongoing growth and development; and 4) providing the early childhood workforce with initial training and professional learning opportunities to build competencies that advance equity, diversity, inclusion and belonging. CDEC’s Division of Early Childhood Workforce leads these efforts through coordinated implementation across the following teams: Professional Learning and Design: The Professional Learning and Design team provides leadership to ensure every member of the early care and education workforce can access required training and continue their growth through high- quality learning opportunities. This team designs, develops, and delivers a range of embedded learning supports for new and practicing early childhood professionals, including virtual instructor-led, self-paced online learning, hybrid training programs, training-of-trainer curricula, mentoring and coaching programs, and documentation tools that reinforce consistent and quality practices across diverse early learning and development settings. The team focuses on competency- and standards-based approaches for the early childhood workforce to ensure children and families experience a supportive care and education system. Registry and Career Pathways: The Registry and Career Pathways team provides leadership to build the infrastructure and systems that support diverse professionals across the early childhood sector through a robust workforce registry, learning management system, and through simplifying and aligning accessible qualification and credentialing pathways. This team works to identify and address barriers to access that exist for individuals who desire a career in Early Childhood Education and to support career advancement pathways through professional credentialing systems that are meaningfully aligned with other CDEC and state programs focused on the early childhood workforce. Activities include managing the ongoing and temporary initiatives to support the continuous growth and development of the early childhood workforce, including the Professional Development Information System (PDIS), Qualification and Competency Alignment Initiatives, and the Early Childhood Professional Credential (ECPC). Workforce Strategy and System Leadership: The Strategy and System Leadership team drives innovation and transformation of the early childhood system through implementation of robust strategies focused on stabilizing, supporting, and growing the EC workforce. This team is deeply engaged in cross agency and stakeholder partners focused on designing responsive alignments with higher education and professional development partners, Early Childhood Councils, funders and other key workforce strategy partners. These include several compensation focused strategies including piloting compensation increase studies, loan forgiveness, scholarship programs and benefits focused initiatives. Activities include leading responsive higher education partnerships for work-based learning (e.g. apprenticeships, credit for prior learning and stackable credentials) and transformative new projects that include designing substitute fund programs, supporting Family, Friend and Neighbor providers and creating learning networks with family child care homes. The Early Childhood Mental Health (ECMH) Consultation: The ECMH team focuses on increasing access to mental health consultants for child care providers and families as well as increased access to professional development and coaching for providers on social-emotional development and behaviors adults find challenging. Specific outputs include a dedicated webpage, Early Childhood Mental Health Consultation, where early childhood providers and caregivers can find information on ECMH consultative services and request services through the online referral. Webpage content includes brief program description, toolkits, as well as links to the EarlyChildhoodMentalHealthCO.org site where customizable print materials, videos and ready-to-post social media graphics that address mental health related topics (stigma, asking for help, etc.) can be accessed by community partners. The PDIS houses a variety of trainings related to social emotional development and ECMH consultation, including Working with an Early Childhood Mental Health Consultant and Recognizing the Impact of Bias in Mental Health Consultation. Additionally, as a means of aligning efforts to reduce suspension and expulsion, the ECMH Program hosts CDEC discussion panels and intentionally networks early childhood support professionals to ensure that a child’s social and emotional needs are identified and addressed early. The program is in the process of creating parent- and provider-facing facts sheets that outline the breadth of services available through consultation and resources that specifically address suspension and expulsion, available in multiple languages. Future workforce activities are outlined in Pathways to Success: Colorado’s Comprehensive Early Childhood Workforce Plan. ii. Developing, maintaining, or implementing early learning and developmental guidelines. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado has a comprehensive set of early learning and developmental guidelines (https://earlylearningco.org/). We will continue to disseminate the early learning and developmental guidelines, using both print and digital dissemination strategies including an updated website. CDEC will update the guidelines if needed, particularly to align with updated Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework or Colorado academic standards, and to be culturally and linguistically responsive. https://earlylearningco.org/ iii. Developing, implementing, or enhancing a quality improvement system. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado is making investments into enhancing the Quality Improvement tracking system as well as maintaining the current QRIS System. Future investments include the implementation of the Universal Preschool Quality Standards (https://cdec.colorado.gov/universal-preschool-colorado) in alignment with the CDEC’s Colorado Shines quality improvement system and the development of a Resource Bank to support providers with quality enhancement efforts. iv. Improving the supply and quality of child care services for infants and toddlers. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado has SLFRF funding to support supply building and capital project support through two grant programs: The Emerging and Expanding grant program and The Employer-Based Child Care grant program. Colorado offers a minor improvement grant supporting infant and toddler programming. Additionally, Colorado uses CCDF funding to support the Expanding Quality for Infants and Toddlers programs, peer mentoring, and coaching initiatives for the infant/toddler workforce. Programs receiving minor improvement grants must attest to continue to enhance or maintain their high-quality rating levels. v. Establishing or expanding a statewide system of CCR&R services. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado will maintain its existing CCR&R network of services and will continue to review options to enhance the search function for families. vi. Facilitating compliance with Lead Agency child care licensing, monitoring, inspection and health and safety standards. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x]Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado will maintain its existing services in child care licensing, monitoring and inspections of health and safety standards and will continue to pursue options to expand licensing services offered in additional languages. vii. Evaluating and assessing the quality and effectiveness of child care services within the State/Territory. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the Colorado Shines quality constructs, a recent evaluation (https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1CxcxNbqHtjV27apzjtlSGPvxKxe3UeBA) of the updated Colorado Shines framework was conducted by Butler Institute for Families, building upon the initial validation conducted by Child Trends in 2018. The report indicates that Colorado Shines standards are aligned to current research and support positive outcomes for children. Next steps are to evaluate feedback to determine how best to make future enhancements. viii. Accreditation support. [x] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [ ] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. ix. Supporting State/Territory or local efforts to develop high-quality program standards relating to health, mental health, nutrition, physical activity, and physical development. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Colorado includes these program standards as part of its QRIS quality standards (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XAJihVcH7YLFG3VlqVxTQ3Q5z0449tVP/view). x. Other activities determined by the Lead Agency to improve the quality of child care services and the measurement of outcomes related to improved provider preparedness, child safety, child well-being, or kindergarten entry. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. -Activities, investments, and staffing to develop, promote and align economic mobility supports and services including coordination and collaboration with county Human Services and Public Health Departments as well as other local partners to support the economic well-being of families. -Supporting the economic wellbeing and opportunities for the advancement of the early childhood workforce. -Build strategies and systems that support children and their families’ smooth transition from early learning experiences (including child care, preschool, Head Start, developmental/Special Education preschool, and/or friend, family, and neighbor care) into kindergarten, ready to learn and to be behaviorally and academically successful. -Investments (FTE, consumer education) to enhance the continuity and strengthen the bridge between child care and kindergarten. -Enhance alignment between senders (early care and learning) and receivers (K-3, local education agency) as children transition between learning environments. -Build coordinated efforts for CCDF and Head Start-eligible children to provide comprehensive child care and developmental services. -Support cross-agency and cross-organizational work through the Quality Nutrition workgroup to expand access to quality nutrition for children in early care and learning settings, including increasing access to CACFP, and expanding access to quality nutrition for families, early childhood providers, and teachers. -Support ongoing access to programs, like the Colorado Early Learning: Universal Design & Inclusion Project and Project Include, that support child care providers in learning how to make adaptations to ensure all children can access a quality early learning environment. -Support CDEC Family Voice Council to ensure they can provide ongoing input into communicating with families around quality child care. -Activities, staff, and investments that support and promote family leadership, education and engagement such as the Family Voice Council, Family Engagement Framework promotion, and other activities. -Maintaining and expanding the use of the Raising Colorado Kids Guide website to promote family connection to supportive early childhood services. -Invest in a Language Justice Coordinator to develop and implement a Department-wide language justice plan and work with external partners to improve engagement with limited English proficient communities. -Diversify community engagement by building strategies and supports to offer and provide interpretation and translation services and culturally responsive practices. -Contribute and participate in external engagement opportunities that promote our engagement with diverse communities. -Engage external partners to serve as thought partners and a sounding board to improve diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility initiatives and strategies by supporting ongoing Tribal Advisory Council work and establishing an DEIA Advisory board inclusive of community working groups, such as Black children and families, Limited English Proficient Families, and Migrant and Refugee Families. -Support ongoing professional development opportunities to increase awareness of diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility especially opportunities that impact historically marginalized communities. -Build coordinated and strategic efforts for cross-agency and cross-organizational work through developing a statewide equity plan that provides a framework for DEIA implementation in early childhood spaces, inclusive of language justice planning and implementation. 8 Lead Agency Coordination and Partnerships to Support Service Delivery Coordination and partnerships help ensure that the Lead Agency’s efforts accomplish CCDF goals effectively, leverage other resources, and avoid duplication of effort. Such coordination and partnerships can help families better access child care, can assist in providing consumer education to parents, and can be used to improve child care quality and the stability of child care providers. Such coordination can also be particularly helpful in the aftermath of disasters when the provision of emergency child care services and the rebuilding and restoring of child care infrastructure are an essential part of ensuring the well-being of children and families in recovering communities. This section identifies who the Lead Agency collaborates with to implement services, how match and maintenance-of-effort (MOE) funds are used, coordination with child care resource and referral (CCR&R) systems, and efforts for disaster preparedness and response plans to support continuity of operations in response to emergencies.
